title: Four protective meditations
hookLine: phone, keys, wallet. and four short thoughts for the road.
tomorrow: forty ways to meditate. why so many, and which one is yours?

lines: THE BUDDHA. KINDNESS. THE BODY. DEATH.
cards: Phone, keys, wallet: the little pat-down at the front door. Which four thoughts could go out the door with you as easily? Theravada practice keeps a set for exactly that, called the four protections.
Each one takes about a breath. The Buddha. Kindness.
The body. Death. That last one sounds heavy for a Tuesday morning.
Stay with it; it turns out to be the one that makes the other three matter.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA: IT CAN BE DONE.
teach.b: Each one is a short form of a longer subject from the forty. First, the Buddha. The old recollection begins, in Pali, Iti pi so Bhagava: such indeed is the Blessed One, worthy, fully awakened.
It's a reminder that a person once did this, so it can be done.

teach.h: KINDNESS: MAY ALL BEINGS BE WELL.
teach.b: Second, kindness: may all beings be well, the heart of the metta practice.

teach.h: THE BODY: HAIR, NAILS, TEETH, SKIN.
teach.b: Third, the body, seen plainly through its parts: hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, skin. Not to hate it; to loosen vanity and wanting.
Fourth, death: certain to come, its time unknown.
One way to see why they travel as a set: they cover the mind from four sides. Confidence, against losing heart. Warmth, against ill will.
Plainness, against vanity. And urgency, against putting off what matters. The fourth is the one that gives the others weight.
If the time is unknown, today's kindness can't wait for a better day.

how: In Theravada practice the four protections (recollection of the Buddha, loving-kindness, the unattractive parts of the body and mindfulness of death) can be done briefly each day, sometimes before a longer sitting, as a short form of the fuller subjects.

four guardian kings who watch the four directions
four quick reflections: Buddha, kindness, body, death

games.q: one finger each — tap the pairs.
p: a person did it, so it can be done
certain to come, its time unknown

s: the four protections are a lucky charm against accidents
they're reflections. what they guard is the mind: against losing heart, ill will, vanity and putting things off.
each one is a short form of a longer meditation subject
recollecting the Buddha, metta, the body's parts and mindfulness of death are all among the forty.
the body reflection is meant to make you hate your body
it sees the body plainly through its parts, to loosen vanity and wanting, not to hate it.

games.q: a friend gets furious at other drivers every single morning on the way to work. which of the four protections is aimed most squarely at that?
o: the body: hair, nails, teeth, skin.
kindness: may all beings be well, that driver too.
the Buddha: such indeed is the Blessed One.
games.why: the four cover the mind from four sides. warmth is the one set against ill will.

practice: Touch your thumb to your first finger: the Buddha, awake, so it can be done. Middle finger: may all beings be well. Ring finger: hair, nails, teeth, skin.
Little finger: death is certain, the time unknown. Then go round the hand again, slower, letting each touch carry its thought.

wordCard.voice: Four protective meditations: the Buddha, kindness, the body's nature, and death. Four short reflections that fit on one hand.

orig.note: Pali: the four protections, the name for this short daily set.

carryVoice: Keep close: four protections, one per finger, ready at any door. Day thirty-nine of the forty, done.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 11.12 and elsewhere (recollection of the Buddha: iti pi so bhagava araham sammasambuddho...)
Sutta Nipata 1.8, Karaniya Metta Sutta (may all beings be happy and secure)
Majjhima Nikaya 10 (the parts of the body, beginning hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, skin); Anguttara Nikaya 6.19 (mindfulness of death)
Visuddhimagga 3 and 7-8 (recollection of the Buddha, loving-kindness, foulness and mindfulness of death among the forty subjects)
